name: Celtic Languages (Genus Template)

formality.description: Celtic languages generally use register-based formality rather than strict T-V pronominal systems. Welsh has ti/chi (informal/formal 'you'), Irish uses universal 'tú', and Scottish Gaelic uses 'thu/sibh'. Formality is primarily expressed through vocabulary choice and discourse markers rather than extensive verb conjugation.

gender.inclusiveGuidance: Celtic languages have masculine/feminine grammatical gender affecting nouns, adjectives, and initial mutations. No neuter gender. Gender-inclusive language conventions are still developing in Celtic languages.

linguisticChallenges.initialMutations: All Celtic languages have systems of initial consonant mutations (lenition, nasalization, aspiration) triggered by grammatical context. A word's first consonant changes based on what precedes it. This is the #1 source of MT errors in Celtic languages.
linguisticChallenges.vsoWordOrder: Celtic languages are Verb-Subject-Object (VSO), one of the rarest word orders globally. Most MT models default to SVO assumptions, producing unnatural Celtic output.
linguisticChallenges.prepositionConjugation: Celtic languages conjugate prepositions — prepositions inflect for person and number (e.g., Irish: agam 'at-me', agat 'at-you', aige 'at-him'). This is typologically unusual and not handled by most MT architectures.

contactInfluences.notes: Progressive replacement of Celtic languages in public domains. All Celtic languages are in various stages of revitalization against English dominance.
Religious and scholarly borrowings from Latin via early Christianity.

notes: Genus template for Insular Celtic languages (Goidelic: Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Manx; Brythonic: Welsh, Breton, Cornish). All share VSO word order, initial mutations, and preposition conjugation.
